title: Stone, tile and grout cleaning and sealing boundaries
audience: Cleaners who clean stone and tile floors and grout, and who need to know where sealing is outside routine cleaning.
learningOutcomes: Choose a pH-appropriate method for stone, tile and grout.
Explain why sealing and stone restoration are outside routine cleaning.
Record the limits of cleaning where grout or stone is stained or etched.

instruction.heading: Stone, tile and grout: what each one is
instruction.body: Natural stone such as marble, limestone and travertine is calcium-based, and an acid will etch it. Granite and slate are often described as less reactive to acid than marble, but this lesson does not confirm that for any particular stone, and a product that is not made for stone can still dull a polished finish. Honed, polished and textured finishes behave differently. A polished surface shows dullness and scratches most easily, and an abrasive pad can remove the polish. Tile is usually more tolerant than stone. Glazed ceramic and porcelain tiles have a hard, fired surface, but the glaze can still be marked by some products, and an abrasive pad can scratch it. Unglazed quarry tile and some porcelain have a more open surface that takes up soil more readily. Grout is the porous material between tiles. Cement-based grout is absorbent and can take up soil, oils and coloured liquids. Epoxy grout is less absorbent and more resistant to staining, but it can still be damaged by the wrong product or a harsh abrasive. Check the product's compatibility with both the tile and the grout before you use it.

instruction.heading: Choosing a method and a brush
instruction.body: Confirm the stone or tile type and the grout before you choose a product, and use the identification steps from “Hard floor identification: timber, stone, tile, vinyl, concrete” where the type is unclear. Where the stone is natural, use a stone-compatible product from the approved list and keep acidic products off it. Where the tile is glazed, use a product that is compatible with the glaze and the grout. Test the product on an inconspicuous area, and wait for the time the label gives before you judge the result. Use a brush that suits the grout and the surface. A soft or medium nylon brush is a common choice for grout lines, and a soft cloth or a non-scratching pad suits polished stone. Do not use a steel brush, steel wool or a harsh abrasive on stone or grout, because the scratch marks hold soil and will make the next clean harder. Work in small sections and rinse as the product label directs. Remove the rinse water as you go, so that residue does not dry on the surface or film over the grout. Do not mix products. Some combinations can release hazardous gases or cause a dangerous reaction. Use one product at a time, and rinse the area between products when the label requires it.

instruction.heading: Sealing, polishing and restoration are outside routine cleaning
instruction.body:
Sealing, polishing, honing, re-grouting and stone restoration all change the surface, the grout or the finish. They are specialist tasks and are outside routine cleaning. A cleaner records the condition of the grout and the stone, and refers any request to seal, polish or restore. Do not promise that a stain will come out, and do not describe a floor as sealed, polished or restored unless that work was carried out and recorded under a defined scope.

Deep grout staining and stone etching may not respond to routine cleaning. Record these as limits of the clean, with photographs taken in shade and under a light held low. Tell the client that the stain or etch may need a specialist assessment, and that the cleaning does not change the underlying condition. This keeps the record accurate and protects the business from a claim that a cleaning step caused or repaired a defect.

procedure: Confirm the stone or tile type and the grout before choosing a product, and record the result.
Avoid acidic products on natural stone, and check that the product is compatible with the tile and grout.
Use one product at a time, test it on an inconspicuous area, and wait for the label time.
Use a soft or medium nylon brush for grout, and a soft cloth or non-scratching pad for polished stone.
Work in small sections, rinse as the label directs, and remove the rinse water as you go.
Record deep stains, grout staining and etch marks as limits of the clean, and photograph them.
Refer sealing, polishing, re-grouting and restoration as specialist work, and record the request.

workedExamples.situation: A client asks you to use an acidic descaler on a polished marble entrance because of white marks.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What do you do before you use any product?
workedExamples.reasoning: Refuse the acidic descaler on marble. Explain that acid can etch the stone, and that the white marks may be a surface change that a cleaner should not try to remove. Check the stone type, use a stone-compatible product from the approved list on a small area, and record the marks as found with photographs. If the marks do not respond, record the limit and refer the floor for specialist assessment.

workedExamples.situation: A client asks you to seal the grout and polish the marble after the clean, as part of the same visit.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What do you say, and what do you record?
workedExamples.reasoning: Explain that sealing and polishing change the surface and are specialist tasks outside routine cleaning. Do not carry them out as part of the clean. Record the request with the date, the area and the client's words. Offer to refer the request to a qualified service after the cleaning is complete, and note that the clean does not change the condition of the grout or the stone.

workedExamples.situation: Dark staining sits deep in the grout lines of a kitchen splashback, and the first approved product lifts only the surface.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: How do you record the result and the limit?
workedExamples.reasoning: Do not switch to a harsher product or a steel brush. Record that the surface film has been removed and that the deeper staining remains. Photograph the grout in shade with a light held low, note the product and the contact time used, and tell the client the deeper stain may need specialist assessment. Do not promise that the staining will come out.

equipmentAndPpe: Stone-compatible and tile-compatible products, each with its label and SDS on hand.
Soft or medium nylon grout brush and soft cloths.
Non-scratching pad approved for polished stone.
Bucket and clean rinse water, with a means of removing rinse water as you go.
Gloves and eye protection as the SDS requires.
Torch or work light held low across the surface for recording condition.

commonErrors.error: Using an acidic descaler on marble or another calcium-based stone.
commonErrors.prevention: Use a stone-compatible product only, and refuse acid on natural stone.

commonErrors.error: Scrubbing grout with a steel brush or a harsh abrasive.
commonErrors.prevention: Use a soft or medium nylon brush and an approved product, and rinse as the label directs.

commonErrors.error: Mixing two products to get a stronger result.
commonErrors.prevention: Use one product at a time, and rinse between products where the label requires it.

commonErrors.error: Promising to seal, polish or restore the floor during a clean.
commonErrors.prevention: Refer sealing and restoration, and record the request and the limits of the clean.

commonErrors.error: Leaving rinse water to dry on the stone or in the grout.
commonErrors.prevention: Remove rinse water as you work, and check the surface after it dries.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Keep the SDS for every product you use, and make sure workers can get at it easily. Safe Work Australia states that copies of SDS must be kept for chemicals used in the hazardous chemical register, and that SDS must be easily accessible to workers who use, handle or store the chemical (no date shown).

Dry-grinding, dry-sweeping and compressed-air cleaning of grout, tile and stone dust can release fine particles, which may include crystalline silica. The national guide for working with silica (February 2022) advises wet methods and warns against dry sweeping and compressed air for dusty surfaces. Where grout or stone work creates dust, check the SDS and the work method first.
Sealing, polishing, grout replacement and stone restoration are outside this course.
Product-specific dilution, dwell time and PPE come from the product label and SDS.

qualityStandard: The stone or tile type and the grout are identified or recorded as unidentified before product selection, in the practical.
An acidic product is refused on natural stone in the case study, and a stone-compatible product is used instead.
The grout is cleaned with a suitable brush and the rinse water is removed, with no harsh abrasive used.
Sealing, polishing or restoration requests are referred and recorded, and are not performed as part of the clean.
documentationEvidence: Floor and grout condition record with the material type, the finish and the photographs.
Product test record for the area tested and the result.
Referral record for any sealing, polishing or restoration request, with the date and the client's words.
Limits of the clean, recorded as found, with the client's acknowledgement.
summary: Identify the stone or tile and the grout before choosing a product.
Keep acid off natural stone, and avoid harsh abrasives on stone and grout.
Sealing, polishing and restoration are referred and recorded, not performed as part of the clean.

knowledgeChecks.question: Why is an acidic product avoided on marble?
options: It has a strong smell that lingers in the room
It can etch the stone and leave dull marks
It is too expensive for a routine clean
It makes the grout expand and crack later

knowledgeChecks.question: A client asks you to seal and polish a floor during a clean. What is correct?
options: Do it as part of the clean, because it is quick and the client will be pleased
Seal a small section with a spray and see how it looks before the rest
Refer it as specialist work outside routine cleaning, and record the request
Polish it with the cleaning product, since the shine will last longer

knowledgeChecks.question: How should a harsh abrasive or steel brush be treated on grout and stone?
options: Use it freely to save time on the clean and finish the room faster
Use it only at the edges of the room, where the grout is most worn
Avoid it, because it can scratch the stone and wear the grout and tile
Use it only after an acid has been applied, since the acid softens the grout
